clue.text: Company doctor meant to tickle you

parts.note: co. is the abbreviation printed after a firm's name
a medic is a doctor, especially an army one

explanation.surface: A firm's own doctor whose bedside manner is designed to make you laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company doctor' is a single job on the surface and two separate crossword pieces underneath, the firm and the man. The definition has to be an adjective because the answer is one.
explanation.definitionFit: Something comedic is intended to raise a laugh, and to tickle somebody is to amuse them, so the definition is that intent spelt out.

clue.text: Bawdy cover of epic novel in enigmatic language

indicators.note: in means the shuffled letters go inside the other word

parts.note: a code is language made deliberately obscure

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: The jacket of an epic novel written in some cryptic tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the book itself, but it means new and rearranges the letters of epic, which sit inside CODE.
explanation.definitionFit: A codpiece was the conspicuous pouch covering the crotch on men's breeches, a famously ribald garment.

clue.text: Earth welcomes alien back with less fanfare, perhaps

indicators.note: welcomes means the earth takes the alien inside it

parts.note: mud is wet earth

indicators.note: back means the alien's letters are read from the end

parts.note: ET is the alien of the Spielberg film

explanation.surface: Planet Earth greets a returning alien without much celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: Muted means subdued or toned down, as a reception is when it lacks fuss and trumpets.

clue.text: Water-resistant barrier strip at the bottom? For sure!

definitions.note: A damp-proof course is a thing and 'Water-resistant' is the property it is laid for; the setter names the layer by the job it does rather than by what it is, so an adjective stands in for a noun.

parts.note: a dam is the barrier built across a valley to hold water back

indicators.note: 'at the bottom' picks out the letter standing at the foot of the word beside it, this being a clue that reads downwards

parts.note: the letter at the foot of STRIP
somebody for a motion is pro it
'Of course!' is the everyday answer that means the same as 'sure!'

explanation.surface: Someone confirming that yes, there is a waterproof strip along the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation at the end splits in two, 'for' becoming pro and 'sure' becoming of course, which is where nine of the fifteen letters come from. Builders lay this layer a few courses above the ground so damp cannot rise past it.
explanation.definitionFit: A damp-proof course is the impervious strip set into a wall near the ground precisely to stop water rising through the brickwork.

clue.text: Balls Welshman put where cow's tail should go

indicators.note: put where means the Welshman's name is placed in a spot belonging to something else
tail is the last letter of the animal, and the name goes there instead

parts.note: the word cow itself, from cow's
Jones is a typically Welsh surname

explanation.surface: A rude command to a Welshman about where to put a cow's tail.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail of COW is its W; JONES takes its place. The answer is Spanish slang that has entered English.
explanation.definitionFit: Cojones is Spanish slang for testicles, used in English to mean courage or nerve.

clue.text: King Charles sounded decent hitting balls with a mallet

parts.note: CR is the royal cypher, Charles Rex, stamped on postboxes since 2022

indicators.note: 'sounded' asks for what a word sounds like rather than how it is written, so the letters that follow are spelt to match a noise

parts.note: decent means okay, and those five letters are the French-looking way of writing that noise

explanation.surface: The King sounding perfectly respectable while knocking balls about the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail of the word is French spelling for an English sound: -quet is said 'kay', the way bouquet is. CR replaced ER as the royal cypher when Elizabeth died.
explanation.definitionFit: Croquet is the lawn game in which balls are driven through hoops with a mallet, so the definition simply describes the play.

clue.text: Rustic riven slate cladding that's remarkable to Mrs Broon

indicators.note: cladding is the covering laid over the face of a building, so the letters on either side are covering what sits between them

parts.note: seven letters run unbroken through these three words, starting on the last letter of the first and stopping on the first letter of the third

explanation.surface: Split slate used as cladding on a rustic building, and what Mrs Broon makes of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Broons are the Scottish comic-strip family who have run in the Sunday Post since 1936, and Maw Broon is the mother of the house. 'Riven' is the real trade term for slate split by hand, which is what keeps the letters innocent.
explanation.definitionFit: Crivens is the Scots cry of astonishment, the exclamation a Broon lets out when something has taken her by surprise.

clue.text: Rail or boat, my two substitutes for route around city

indicators.note: substitutes are the players sent on in place of others, and every letter here ends up standing in somebody else's place

parts.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters

explanation.surface: Two stand-ins offered instead of rail or boat for getting round a city.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything before 'substitutes' is raw material, fifteen letters of it, which is why the transport words read as a list of travel options rather than as letters. London's M25 is the orbital motorway everybody means.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbital motorway is the ring of dual carriageway thrown round a city to carry traffic past it instead of through it.

clue.text: Bad article in Le Monde, stupid and totally lacking conclusions

parts.note: une is the French feminine indefinite article, as in Le Monde, a French newspaper

indicators.note: lacking means going without, here without the ending of the word for stupid

parts.note: thick means stupid

indicators.note: the plural conclusions means the word for totally loses its last letter as well

parts.note: all means totally, as in all alone

explanation.surface: A newspaper critic complaining about a dim, inconclusive article in a French daily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conclusions' is plural, so both THICK and ALL lose their final letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Unethical behaviour is morally wrong, bad in the sense of wicked.

clue.text: I appreciate that knowledge is taught

parts.note: ta is the British thank-you, said when somebody has done you a good turn
ken is knowledge — beyond your ken is beyond what you know

explanation.surface: Somebody glad to hear that the subject is on the syllabus.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage the person who takes a class is the one conducting it, which is the sense the definition needs. 'I appreciate that' is a whole phrase standing in for two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesson or a service taken by somebody is one they conduct, so in British usage what is taken is what is taught.

clue.text: Statistician's figure beginning to develop a paunch

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is the letter it starts with, and that single letter is all this hands over

parts.note: the opening letter of DEVELOP
the word a, taken as it stands
tum is the nursery word for the stomach, and a paunch is a fat one

explanation.surface: A statistician starting to put on weight round the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' is a body on the surface and a number underneath, which is the whole disguise. Datum is the singular of data, one reading rather than the set, so the definition is singular too.
explanation.definitionFit: A datum is a single recorded value, one figure in the table a statistician works from.

clue.text: Running out of porridge?

definitions.meaning: read straight, having none of it left in the cupboard; read the setter's way, making a run for it
read straight, the oats boiled for breakfast; read the setter's way, British slang for a stretch in prison

explanation.surface: The kitchen cupboard turns out to be empty at breakfast time.
explanation.walkthrough: Porridge for a prison sentence is British slang, fixed in the language by the 1970s sitcom of that name with Ronnie Barker. Both halves of the phrase turn over at once, which is what lets it read so innocently.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody serving porridge who runs out of it has got out of jail, so the phrase describes the escape in the slang of the place.

clue.text: Dine out and write down impression without bias

indicators.note: out means the letters are put out of order

parts.note: to pen something is to write it down
a dent is an impression left in a surface

explanation.surface: Instructions for a restaurant reviewer: eat out and record your impressions fairly.
explanation.definitionFit: Independent means not influenced by others, impartial and free from partisanship.

clue.text: Darling usually left tap running

parts.note: taps are marked H and C, and the H is the one usually fitted on the left
an engine that is running is on

explanation.surface: A darling who has gone off and left the hot tap running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Usually' is the setter owning up: the hot tap is only conventionally the left-hand one, which is enough to fix the letter without pretending it is a rule. Hon is the clipped form of honey.
explanation.definitionFit: Hon is short for honey, the endearment you call somebody instead of using their name.

clue.text: Unmoved listening to great soprano

indicators.note: listening to a name means taking the sound of it, so what you write down is spelt to match what you hear

parts.note: Maria Callas was the great operatic soprano of the last century, and her name said aloud is spelt out here another way

explanation.surface: Somebody left cold by a recording of a great soprano.
explanation.walkthrough: Maria Callas, the Greek-American diva who died in 1977, is the soprano crosswords mean. 'Soprano' is the trap for practised solvers, who expect it to hand over an S and nothing more.
explanation.definitionFit: Callous means hardened and unfeeling, the state of being unmoved by what would move anybody else.

clue.text: Metal frame in the door improved security for Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner was the Oxford don known for swapping the starting sounds of words

parts.note: better means improved
locks give security on a door

explanation.surface: An upgrade to a front door's metalwork for the sake of security.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of BETTER LOCKS and you hear the answer; the second word is only said, not spelt, as BOX.
explanation.definitionFit: A letterbox is the slot with a hinged metal flap in a front door through which post is delivered.

clue.text: Sympathise with expert behind following that learner driver

indicators.note: what stands behind something comes after it, so the expert takes the back of the answer rather than the front

parts.note: 'following that' is therefore, and therefore is so
the L-plate a learner driver hangs on the car
an ace at something is an expert at it

explanation.surface: Sympathy for the expert driver stuck behind a learner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following that' reads as a position in the queue and is doing the work of 'therefore' instead. The L-plate is the white square with a red L that British learners hang front and back.
explanation.definitionFit: To solace somebody is to comfort them in their distress, which is fellow feeling turned into something you actually do.

clue.text: Awful gag inside the 11 had

indicators.note: inside means within, so what is named before it drops into the middle of what is named after

parts.note: 11 across is the paper this crossword is printed in, and a paper says 'we' of itself, so 'we had' shortens to we'd
to gag on something is to retch

explanation.surface: A dreadful joke that ran inside the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is the setter winking at his own paper: 11 across is the Independent. The apostrophe of 'we'd' is simply dropped, as punctuation always may be.
explanation.definitionFit: Wretched means miserably poor in quality, which is 'awful' in the sense of a thing not worth the paper rather than of something frightening.

clue.text: Cons row on board ship

indicators.note: what is on board a vessel is inside it, so the quarrel goes within the two letters that stand for the ship

parts.note: SS is the prefix painted on a steamship's name
a tiff is a small row

explanation.surface: Convicts having a row aboard a prison ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cons' looks like the convicts of the surface and is a verb in the definition. SS opens up to take the quarrel, which is the only way six letters come out of a four-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: To stiff somebody is to cheat them out of what they are owed — walking out on the bill is stiffing the waiter.

clue.text: Train not on schedule, perhaps ice blocking circuits up?

indicators.note: something blocking a passage is stuck in the middle of it, so these letters lodge inside the others
in a clue that reads down the grid, up means the letters are taken from the foot of the column back to the top

parts.note: a circuit of the track is a lap
the word itself, dropped in as it stands

explanation.surface: Ice on the line blocking the signal circuits and holding a train up.
explanation.walkthrough: The turn comes after the insertion, so all seven letters go round together rather than either piece on its own. A special is a train laid on outside the timetable, for a race meeting or a football crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A special is a train put on outside the published timetable, so by definition it is not one you will find on the schedule.

clue.text: Busy type bags excess drugs left in untidy drawer

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it away in a bag, so the busy type closes round the letters named next

parts.note: a doer is somebody who gets on with things rather than talking about them
an OD is an overdose
l = left

explanation.surface: An energetic sort pocketing surplus pills left lying in a messy drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawer' is the furniture on the surface and one who draws in the definition, which is the whole disguise. OD for overdose is worth owning: it turns up wherever a clue mentions too many drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawer is one who draws, and a doodler draws absent-mindedly — untidy scribbles down the margin rather than anything composed.

clue.text: Widow earned money in bar to the north

indicators.note: 'in' drops what is named before it inside what is named after
north is up the page, and a clue reading down the grid that is read northwards has its letters in the other order

parts.note: a rod is a metal bar
the money earned for a week's work is a wage

explanation.surface: A widow who came into money working in a bar somewhere up north.
explanation.walkthrough: A dowager holds her title from a dead husband: the dowager duchess is the old duke's widow, as against the new duke's wife. The bar is turned round before the wage goes into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowager is a widow left holding the title and the property of her late husband, which is why the word still arrives with a duchess attached.

clue.text: Nobleman denied king's reward

indicators.note: to be denied something is to have it withheld from you, so the letter named next never arrives

parts.note: a duke is a nobleman, the highest rank below the royals
k = king, the letter that is withheld

explanation.surface: A nobleman refused the reward the king had promised him.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as 'is', which is what turns a slighted nobleman into an equation. Your due is what is coming to you, as in giving a man his due.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody's due is what they have earned and are owed, so a reward that is due to a person is that reward itself.

clue.text: A bit of delusion concerning in the morning?

definitions.text: A bit of delusion concerning in the morning?

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a piece of it, and the piece a clue asks for in these words is the letter it opens with

parts.note: the opening letter of DELUSION
re is the 'concerning' at the head of a memo
am is ante meridiem, before noon

explanation.surface: A touch of self-deception, and worrying to find it there first thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, the whole clue describes what its own letters spell, which is what &lit means. 'Concerning' carries the modern worrying sense on the surface and the memo-heading sense in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a dream is a scrap of delusion that visits you while you sleep and is still with you when morning comes.

clue.text: Highly stressed wife rude in public

indicators.note: 'in' puts everything named before it inside what is named after, so both short pieces land in the middle of the long word

parts.note: an overt act is one done in the open, in public
w = wife
rough language is rude language

explanation.surface: A wife behaving rudely in public and working herself into a state.
explanation.walkthrough: OVERT is prised open between its fourth and fifth letters, which is the hard part: five-letter words are usually kept whole. Overwrought is literally over-worked, from the old past participle of 'work'.
explanation.definitionFit: Overwrought means worked up past the point of control, the state of nerves that 'highly stressed' names in newer words.

clue.text: Eccentric gay eats Dorothy's country dumplings

indicators.note: eats means the scrambled letters take the next piece inside them
eccentric means odd, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Oz is the land Dorothy visits in The Wizard of Oz

explanation.surface: An eccentric gay man tucking into dumplings from Dorothy's homeland.
explanation.definitionFit: Gyoza are Japanese pan-fried dumplings, often stuffed with pork and cabbage.

clue.text: Loading bananas, half of them in the van

indicators.note: the van is the vanguard, the front of an advancing army, so whatever is in the van goes first

parts.note: the back half of THEM; the front half would not join onto what follows
bananas and barking both mean mad

explanation.surface: Loading crates of bananas, half of them stacked up front in the van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van' is the delivery vehicle on the surface and the vanguard in the instruction, the front of an army on the march. Barking is short for barking mad, which is where bananas comes in.
explanation.definitionFit: To embark cargo or troops is to put them aboard ship, so loading is the same operation named from the quayside.

clue.text: Furious when gold reverts in value

indicators.note: in means the change happens inside the word for value

parts.note: worth is value

indicators.note: reverts here means turns back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Someone enraged when the gold price falls back.
explanation.walkthrough: Gold here is the heraldic word, and 'reverts in' says its two letters turn round where they already sit inside the word for value.
explanation.definitionFit: Wroth is an old literary word for angry, full of wrath.

clue.text: Most healthy physicist

parts.note: max is short for maximum, the most there is
somebody healthy is well

explanation.surface: A physicist in the very best of health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most' reads as an adverb propping up 'healthy' and is a noun doing its own work. Both halves are ordinary words, so there is no odd letter to give the join away.
explanation.definitionFit: James Clerk Maxwell, whose equations tied electricity, magnetism and light together, is one of the great physicists, so the definition names his trade and leaves you the man.

clue.text: Fox nearly squished leaving large road

indicators.note: squished means crushed out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
leaving means the letter for large is taken out of the jumble

parts.note: taken as written for the jumble
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A fox that was almost run over as it left a big road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' looks like almost, but it is the anagram fodder: without its L the letters make REYNA.
explanation.definitionFit: Reynard is the traditional name of the fox in medieval fables, used as a literary name for any fox.
